segments.title: Lucilla's Drawing Room: The Architecture of Social Power

utterances.text: Welcome to Miss Marjoribanks Unpacked — a deep dive into one of the most dazzling, underappreciated novels of the Victorian era.
Mrs Oliphant published Miss Marjoribanks in 1866, and it remains a masterclass in comic irony, social ambition, and the quiet ferocity of a woman determined to run the world on her own terms.
I'm your host, and today we're joined by three guests who have thought long and hard about this extraordinary book.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is forensically interested in how great fiction is built — sentence by sentence, image by image.
Professor James Blackstone brings a legal and social historian's eye — the real institutions behind the fiction, the stakes that Oliphant's contemporaries would have felt in their bones.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Miss Marjoribanks as a teenager and has never quite recovered — in the best possible sense.
She is our guide to what it feels like to actually read this novel — the jokes, the aches, the sentences you have to read twice.
Our opening question is about the thing that drives the whole novel: Lucilla Marjoribanks and the drawing room she has turned into a theatre of power.
Eleanor, let's start with you — because Oliphant's craft is everywhere in how she renders Lucilla managing people.
What strikes me first is the economy — the absolute ruthlessness of compression Oliphant brings to her social scenes.
There's a moment in chapter thirty-two that I think is one of the finest examples of character-in-action in the whole novel.
Lucilla introduces two men to each other, dismisses one of them almost before the sentence is finished, and then pivots to flatter the other — all in about forty words.
Here it is:
"The Archdeacon wants to make your acquaintance. Mr Cavendish — Mr Beverley. There, you know each other."
And then, immediately — 'when we are gone you can talk to each other if you like, but in the meantime you are too far off, and I want the Archdeacon.'
'There, you know each other' — that 'there' does the work of a whole paragraph.
It's the sound of a woman tidying up a social problem and moving on, brisk as closing a drawer.
And Oliphant lets you hear the velvet over the iron — 'He is so much liked in Carlingford' — flattery deployed with surgical precision.
That 'there' really is extraordinary — it sounds almost maternal, and yet it's completely imperious.
James, from a social historian's point of view — what is actually at stake when Lucilla manages a room like this?
What's at stake is very real, and I think modern readers sometimes miss just how constrained Lucilla's formal options are.
She cannot vote, she cannot stand for Parliament, she cannot enter most of the professions — the drawing room is not a consolation prize, it is literally the only arena available to her.
And so when Lucilla engineers introductions, steers conversations, manages who sits where and who speaks to whom — she is doing politics.
The Archdeacon is a figure of considerable ecclesiastical and social weight in a Victorian town like Carlingford.
The fact that Lucilla places herself beside him — 'I want the Archdeacon' — and uses his presence to anchor the evening is a genuine piece of social strategy.
Not decoration. Not hostessing. Strategy.
What I love is that Oliphant never lets Lucilla be merely strategic — there is always this shimmer of genuine feeling underneath.
And nowhere is that more moving than when Mr Cavendish returns, and Lucilla has to reckon with what he once meant to her.
Oliphant gives us this passage that I find genuinely tender — let me read it.

"She would not have been human if she had heard without emotion of the return of the man whom she had once dreamed of as member for Carlingford, with the addition of other dreams which had not been altogether without their sweetness."
'Dreams which had not been altogether without their sweetness' — that double negative is so carefully restrained.
Oliphant will not let Lucilla be sentimental, and yet the feeling is unmistakably there.
She dreams of him as a parliamentary candidate first, and a romantic prospect second — and that order tells you everything about who Lucilla is.
That's exactly right, and the passage just before it is where Oliphant shows us Lucilla's composure as a kind of armour she has to consciously put on.
When her father brings her the newspaper with the news of Cavendish's return, Lucilla says:
"Thank you all the same, papa, for bringing me the paper. It would have been a great deal worse if I had not known of it before I saw him."
That 'a great deal worse' is the sentence of a woman who has learned to manage her own interior as rigorously as she manages her drawing room.
She needs preparation time — not to suppress the feeling, but to arrange it into something she can function inside of.
The craft here is that Oliphant makes us understand this in one line of dialogue — no interiority spelled out, no authorial intrusion.
There is something historically significant in that sentence too — 'I am sure I am very glad for one thing: he can't be married or dead, as people used to say.'
The casual yoking of marriage and death as equivalent social exits for a man from a woman's consideration — that is sharply observed social reality.
For a woman in Lucilla's position, an unmarried man of standing is a live possibility — and a married one is simply gone from the board.
Oliphant renders the marriage market with a kind of clear-eyed bleakness that the comic surface barely conceals.
And yet the novel refuses to end on that bleakness — it ends on Tom.
After all the grand prospects — all the candidates Lucilla has auditioned, consciously or not — it is Tom Marjoribanks who wins her.
And Oliphant gives us this catalogue that is almost biblical in its rhythm:
"after all the archdeacons, doctors, generals, members of Parliament — after the ten years and more in which she had not gone off."
'Had not gone off' — as though Lucilla were a jar of preserves.
It is funny and also devastating — the contempt the world has for a woman who does not marry is captured in three words.
And yet Lucilla has spent those ten years building something — a career in everything but name.
That tension — between what society sees when it looks at Lucilla and what she has actually been doing — feels central to everything the novel is arguing.
Which makes it the perfect moment to turn to how Oliphant uses Lucilla's world to hold a mirror up to the class and propriety structures of Carlingford itself.

segments.title: Society's Mirror: Class, Propriety, and the Marjoribanks Influence

utterances.text: We've been examining how Lucilla constructs her drawing room as a theatre of social power.
Now let's look at what happens when that power is tested — when society tries to impose its own agenda on Lucilla, and she pushes back.
The chapter-eight encounter with Mr Bury is one of the great comic set-pieces in the novel, and it works because Oliphant gives us the machinery of Lucilla's mind in real time.
There's a wonderful moment where Lucilla has what can only be described as a genuine fright — and then, in the space of a breath, recalculates entirely.
The narrator puts it with extraordinary precision:
"Lucilla uttered a scream of genuine alarm and dismay; and then she came to herself, and saw the force of her position."
That pivot — alarm, then clarity, then action — is the essential Lucilla rhythm, and Oliphant compresses it into a single sentence.
It's architecturally perfect: the scream is real, the recovery is real, and neither cancels the other out.
And the Rector's scheme is worth dwelling on for a moment, because it wasn't unusual — not at all.
A widower's household — particularly a prosperous one — was seen as incomplete, potentially improper, and the parish felt a certain proprietary interest in remedying that.
Mr Bury's solution — a respectable widow installed as companion-guardian — was a socially sanctioned move, meant to reassert order.
Oliphant renders that intervention with devastating comic fidelity — the Rector speaks of liberty turning unpleasant, of a 'Christian friend to watch over and take care of you.'
"You may think the liberty is pleasant at first, but if you had a Christian friend to watch over and take care of you——"
The condescension is perfectly calibrated — and of course, it's the 'Christian friend' herself who nearly collapses on the spot.
The institution meant to discipline Lucilla is itself already in disorder before the plan even begins.
What I love about that scene is the way poor Mrs Mortimer becomes a kind of unwilling accomplice in Lucilla's victory — entirely without meaning to.
She nearly faints, and in that fainting she derails the Rector completely.
And Lucilla's response is — well, there's a phrase that stops me every time I read it.
"It was not Lucilla's way to lose time about anything; she took the poor woman by the shoulders and all but lifted her to the sofa."
'All but lifted her to the sofa' — that physical decisiveness is so characteristic, and yet so startling in a Victorian heroine.
She doesn't flutter, she doesn't defer to the man in the room — she just acts.
And the narrator's response to all this is glorious — that droll aside about the Rector's feelings.
She calls what's happened an 'entr'acte which was not in his programme' — treating the whole emergency as a theatrical interruption.
And then she says 'to describe the feelings with which Mr Bury contemplated this little entr'acte would be beyond our powers.'
'Beyond our powers' — meaning the narrator is simply declining to bother.
The Rector's indignation is so irrelevant that it doesn't merit narration.
That is a radical act of narrative authority, and Oliphant pulls it off with total ease.
There's also a sharp social irony in who the Rector has selected as his instrument.
He turns up with a 'candidate' for the household, and Lucilla wrong-foots him immediately with that artless question.
She asks, with a look of perfectly innocent surprise:
"Do you mean you have found some one for him to marry?"
Redirecting the entire proposal toward her father rather than herself — in one clean stroke.
Legally, socially, the Rector has every conventional warrant for his intervention — and she dismantles it with a single, guileless sentence.
But what moves me most is the moment after — once the battle is won.
Lucilla could simply dismiss Mrs Mortimer, having used her as — and the narrator is bracingly honest about this — 'a victim.'
Instead, something genuine surfaces.
The narrator tells us:
"though she had not hesitated to sacrifice this poor woman when it was necessary to have a victim, that moment was over, and she had no pleasure in being cruel."
There's real moral seriousness there — Oliphant doesn't let Lucilla off the hook, but she doesn't condemn her either.
And then she goes and sits with Mrs Mortimer, listens to her story, and is 'more comforting than the Rector could have been for his life.'
That last flourish is quietly devastating — the professional Christian, outclassed in Christian mercy.
It tells you something essential about Oliphant's moral vision — that competence and care are not opposites.
Lucilla is ruthless when she needs to be, and genuinely kind when she can afford to be — and the novel treats both as equally real.
The sentimental Victorian novel would have made her choose one or the other — the schemer or the angel.
Oliphant refuses that binary entirely.
And there's one more dimension to the chapter that I think deserves mention — Tom's proposal.
It comes at the end of a chapter devoted to Lucilla managing every form of external pressure, and it arrives with an almost painful directness.
Tom stumbles over his words, repeats himself, and finally gets there:
"I mean I want you to consent to—to—to—marry me, Lucilla. That is what I mean."
The repeated 'to—to—to' on the page is almost musical — it renders the stammer without caricature.
And then that redundant 'That is what I mean' at the end — as if he doesn't trust himself to have been understood.
Against everything Lucilla has just accomplished in this chapter, that vulnerability is almost unbearably exposed.
Tom is a genuinely sympathetic figure precisely because he is so utterly unlike Lucilla — no strategy, no performance, just longing.
He even wishes he weren't her cousin — as if the family connection were itself a kind of obstacle, a disadvantage in the contest for her attention.
It's comic and heartbreaking at once, which is very much Oliphant's register throughout this novel.
And that combination — comedy and heartbreak sitting side by side — brings us naturally to our next question.
Because Oliphant is doing something quite particular with wit in this novel — Lucilla's comic mode is both her armour and her argument.
That's exactly what we'll be exploring next: the comedy of ambition, and what Lucilla's wit reveals about the novel's larger vision.

segments.title: The Comedy of Ambition: Lucilla's Wit and the Novel's Comic Vision

utterances.text: We've been exploring how Lucilla's Thursdays function as a kind of social architecture — a way of ordering Carlingford around a single will.
But there's another dimension to all that ordering, and it's the one that makes the novel so irresistibly entertaining: Lucilla is genuinely, magnificently funny.
Caroline, you've been rereading these passages, and I know you have strong views on what makes Lucilla's comedy so distinctive.
What strikes me, every time, is that Lucilla is never trying to be funny.
The comedy comes from the absolute sincerity of her egoism — and Oliphant is very precise about the nature of that egoism.
There's a passage in the early chapters that I think is the key to everything.
"Miss Marjoribanks went straight forward, leaving an unquestionable wake behind her, and running down with indifference the little skiffs in her way."
That word "indifference" is doing so much work.
She doesn't maliciously run people down — she simply doesn't notice she's done it.
That's what separates comic egotism from villainy.
That naval metaphor is extraordinary, isn't it — a "wake."
Oliphant is casting Lucilla as a ship of the line moving through a harbour full of small pleasure boats.
There's grandeur in it, but also a structural comedy: ships of the line belong to oceans, not to provincial drawing rooms.
And then Oliphant adds that brilliant qualifier — she notes that Lucilla's course "might be a little deficient in grace" — before immediately dismissing the objection.
"Grace, after all, is but a secondary quality."
That's the narrator adopting Lucilla's own voice — ventriloquising her self-justification — and it's absolutely deadpan.
I'd add that there's something historically specific about that egoism, too.
In mid-Victorian provincial life, a woman of Lucilla's position had essentially no institutional channel for the kind of drive she possesses.
Politics, the professions, the church — all closed.
So she constructs Thursday evenings as a kind of parallel Parliament, with herself as both Prime Minister and chief whip.
The comedy of ambition is inseparable from that structural frustration — and Oliphant knows it.
And when that ambition meets a genuine obstacle, the comedy sharpens into something almost Gothic.
The Mr Cavendish scenes are the best example of this.
There's a moment where Lucilla summons him for a serious talk, and she deploys just a flick of her hand to obliterate Barbara Lake from his consciousness entirely.
The setup is so quiet — she says,

"Hush, don't laugh, please; for I want to have a very serious talk. I have been hearing about you from some very, very old friends, Mr Cavendish — not anything about this, you know," Miss Marjoribanks added, waving her hand in the direction of Grove Street.
And then Oliphant delivers the line that stops me cold every time.
"Barbara Lake and everything connected with her vanished like a shadow from the unfortunate man's mind."
"The unfortunate man." It's devastating — and perfectly comic.
That phrase "vanished like a shadow" is doing double work.
On one level it's pure comic deflation — Barbara Lake, who has been tormenting Cavendish for chapters, simply ceases to exist the moment Lucilla speaks.
But there's something slightly sinister about it, too — a woman reduced to nothing by another woman's social power.
The Gothic note Caroline mentioned is absolutely right.
Lucilla's power over minds has something uncanny about it — and Oliphant never quite lets us forget that.
And the Cavendish plot, when it returns in the later chapters, is a marvellous study in what I can only call political comedy.
Here is a man who has fled Carlingford under — we gather — considerable social pressure, and who chooses to re-enter public life by standing for Parliament.
Oliphant's description of his return is beautifully dry.
"It was actually Mr Cavendish who had come home, and whose address to the electors of Carlingford, dated from Dover on his return to England, the Doctor had just put into his daughter's hand."
"Dated from Dover" — the man can't even get off the boat before he's issuing addresses.
And Lucilla, "though taken unawares, had not given in, nor shown any signs of weakness" — even political surprises are absorbed into the system.
The scene that hits me hardest, though, is much quieter — and it comes very late in the novel.
Aunt Jemima has said something — something that frightens even herself before it's out of her mouth — about someone being fond of Lucilla.
And Lucilla's response is a moment where the comedy and the pathos become genuinely indistinguishable.
"I don't think you know anybody who is fond of me, Aunt Jemima," she said; "I don't suppose anybody is fond of me. Do you?"
She has thrown her embroidery aside and looks Aunt Jemima keenly in the face.
For just a moment, all the machinery of social performance falls away.
And then — of course — it closes again.
That moment is why the comedy never tips into mere satire.
Oliphant keeps opening these small windows — and then letting Lucilla close them herself, with a kind of magnificent self-sufficiency.
We're never quite sure whether she is entirely unconscious of her own vulnerability, or whether she simply refuses to let anyone see it.
That ambiguity is structural — it's built into the narration itself.
There's a social dimension too, I think.
For a woman in Lucilla's position — unmarried, no mother, running a household entirely on her own terms — the question of whether anyone is "fond" of her is not sentimental.
It's existential.
A woman without attachments is, in mid-Victorian provincial society, genuinely exposed — and Lucilla knows it, even if she refuses to show it.
What's remarkable is that Oliphant generates all of this — comedy, pathos, ambiguity — largely through narration: through the voice that frames Lucilla rather than simply recording her.
Which brings us naturally to the question of technique — how Oliphant's ironic narrator shapes what we understand about her characters, and what it withholds.

segments.title: Technique and Irony: Oliphant's Narrative Mastery in Character Revelation

utterances.text: We've been exploring the comic brilliance of Lucilla's ambition — but what makes that comedy land is the precision of the narration surrounding it.
So let's turn now to the craft itself: how Oliphant constructs irony, how she deploys her narrator, and what those choices reveal about character.
One of the things that strikes me most forcibly about Oliphant is how she uses narrative distance as a tool of revelation — not concealment.
The narrator is omniscient, but she chooses the most devastating moments to step close and show us what is actually inside a character.
The opening of the novel gives us this immediately with Dr Marjoribanks at his wife's death.
"A painful heaviness possessed him when he became aware how little real sorrow was in his mind, and how small an actual loss was this loss of his wife."
That word "heaviness" is doing extraordinary work — it is not grief, it is the weight of recognising the absence of grief.
Oliphant gives us a man who is punished not by sorrow but by self-knowledge.
And the comparison to poor Mr Lake the drawing-master is so precisely cruel — that's what makes it linger.
The full sentence goes on to say his wife's loss "bulked before the world as an event of just as much magnitude" as the loss Lake was suffering at the same moment.
Society grants the Doctor the full ceremonial weight of bereavement — and inwardly he knows it is unearned.
There's something almost Tolstoyan in that compression — the gap between the public event and the private reality exposed in one subordinate clause.
The drawing-master is not chosen arbitrarily, of course.
A drawing-master occupies one of the most socially precarious positions in Victorian provincial life — dependent on the patronage of households like the Doctor's, perpetually on the threshold.
To place his loss in the same moral register as the Doctor's is a deliberate provocation from the narrator.
It flattens the social hierarchy at the very moment the Doctor is receiving its deference.
That technique — the narrator levelling the social world with a single comparative clause — appears again in the chapter about the Archdeacon and Mrs Mortimer.
Mr Beverley is a man accustomed to authority, but watch what happens when he is caught off guard.

"Good Heavens, marry him! You must be raving. She would as soon think of — going for a soldier," said Mr Beverley, "with a hoarse and perfectly unmirthful laugh, or doing anything else that was mad and unnatural."
"Perfectly unmirthful" — that is a masterclass in five syllables.
It tells us his laugh is the involuntary convulsion of a man whose composure has entirely failed him.
And the comparison — "going for a soldier" — is so wildly bathetic it reveals exactly how desperate he is to close the subject.
The phrase "mad and unnatural" catches me every time — because it applies, by implication, to any independent desire Mrs Mortimer might have of her own.
Beverley doesn't even register that he's described female agency as categorically insane.
Oliphant lets him condemn himself in his own spluttering syntax.
She never has to editorialize — the character does the work.
There is a structural counterpart to that moment much later in the novel, when the Doctor's financial ruin is revealed.
Oliphant constructs it with the same economy — the will, the reading, and then the collapse, all in three short moves.
The sentence itself enacts the reversal.
"After the will was read, it was found out that everything named in it had disappeared like a bubble.
Instead of being the richest, Dr Marjoribanks was one of the poorest men in Carlingford when he shut his door behind him on that snowy night."
The bubble image is almost too simple — and that is its force.
There is no Gothic machinery of ruin, no theatrical exposure — just a legal instrument that names things that no longer exist.
What I find structurally brilliant about that passage is how it rhymes with the novel's opening.
The Doctor appears first as a man whose inner life is unexpectedly empty; he reappears at the end as a man whose outer prosperity is equally empty.
Oliphant has built a character whose two defining revelations are both about the discovery of absence.
That kind of long-range structural echo takes real architectural confidence.
The narrator's treatment of Cavendish in Chapter 49 has that same quality — that willingness to deliver a verdict with absolute finality.
She sets him up as someone the narrator genuinely mourns over — not mockingly, but with something like exasperation.
The passage calls him
"a man who was capable of so much better things — a man even who, if he had made a right use of his opportunities, might once have had as good a chance as any other of marrying Lucilla herself."
"If he had made a right use of his opportunities" — there is something almost parental in that tone.
The narrator knows exactly what he threw away, and she wants us to feel it too.
That passage is also interesting because of what it says about the marriage market as a system of opportunity.
Cavendish had a "chance" — the novel's language is almost contractual there.
He failed not because the system excluded him, but because he did not manage himself well within it.
Which makes the narrator's judgment both more damning and, in its way, more sympathetic — it was not fate, it was failure.
And then we arrive at what I think is one of the finest single sentences in the whole novel — Lucilla's moment of unprecedented self-ignorance.
Throughout the entire novel Lucilla always knows what she wants — that is practically her defining characteristic.
So when Oliphant writes this, it is seismic.
"For the first time in her life she not only did not know what she would do, but she did not know what she wanted to do."
The syntactic doubling — "not only did not know... but she did not know" — enacts the paralysis.
It is not just that she cannot decide — she cannot even locate the faculty of desire.
For a character this self-possessed, this self-aware, that is genuinely vertiginous.
I reread that sentence every single time I come back to this novel.
Because after four hundred pages of Lucilla knowing everything, that sentence is — there's no other word for it — a rupture.
Oliphant has been building to it all along, but she waits — she waits until the very last possible moment to crack the surface.
That restraint is itself a form of mastery.
And it is precisely at that cracked surface that Cavendish's story intersects with Lucilla's most painfully.
Which brings us to the man whose own failures set so much of the novel's crisis in motion — and what it means when masculine respectability begins to collapse.

segments.title: Cavendish's Fall and the Crisis of Masculine Respectability

utterances.text: We've been talking about Oliphant's ironic narrator — that cool, precise instrument she uses to expose her characters from the inside.
Now I want to turn that lens onto Mr Cavendish — because his rise and wobble in these chapters is where that irony does some of its most interesting work.
What I find so delicious about the Cavendish material is how Oliphant places him in the sights of two very different women simultaneously.
On one side you have Lucilla — fully in command, assessing him with the cool detachment of a general reviewing cavalry.
And on the other, there's Barbara Lake, who sees him in an entirely different register.
Oliphant's line about her is one of those perfect, devastating sentences.
"Barbara had never as yet had a lover, but she had read an unlimited number of novels, which came to nearly the same thing."
That little parenthesis — "which came to nearly the same thing" — is withering and tender at once.
Oliphant doesn't mock Barbara cruelly; she just notes, with perfect precision, exactly what Barbara is working with.
That sentence is doing something technically brilliant, and it's worth pausing on the mechanism.
The qualifying clause — "which came to nearly the same thing" — arrives after a full stop that hasn't quite landed yet.
It has the rhythm of an afterthought, but it carries the entire weight of the joke.
And Oliphant does this repeatedly with Barbara — she's always half a beat behind the real situation, reading life as if it were a three-volume novel.
The irony isn't savage, as Caroline says — but it has teeth.
Because Barbara's misreading will have real consequences for Cavendish's social position — which is where I think things get genuinely interesting.
That word — position — is exactly the right one, and I don't think it's incidental.
Cavendish is described, repeatedly, as the future M.P. for Carlingford — that phrase appears almost like a title.
Parliamentary candidacy in mid-Victorian England was an intensely social project — it required the right connections, the right drawing room, the right wife.
So when Cavendish pays Lucilla that extraordinary compliment — and it is extraordinary — it lands on several registers at once.
"Your conception of social politics, it is masterly."
He's flattering her, yes — but he's also recognising in her something a political man actually needs.
The tragedy — if one wants to call it that — is that he says this to the one woman in Carlingford who is too clear-sighted to be simply pleased by it.
And Lucilla's response to that compliment is wonderfully characteristic — she doesn't blush, she takes a decision.
Or rather, she recognises that a decision may be required of her.
Yes — and that passage about Lucilla assessing the situation is one of the funniest things in the novel.
Oliphant tells us, with a perfectly straight face, that Lucilla has not reached nineteen without receiving what she calls "the natural homage of mankind."
She's experienced — she knows how to crush an unwanted admirer "in the bud," as she intends to do with poor Tom.
But Cavendish is different — and the reason is entirely political, not romantic.
His case, she notices, has "various features peculiar to itself" — which is perhaps the most unsentimental way any heroine has ever considered a proposal.
It made me laugh out loud the first time I read it, and it still does.
What I keep coming back to is the moment where the whole room stops — and I mean that literally.
The duet scene is one of Oliphant's great set pieces — the kind of passage you want to read aloud.
The way she renders that collective arrested moment is almost cinematic in its precision.

"The words were arrested on the very lips of the talkers; Mrs Woodburn paused in the midst of doing Lucilla, and, as we have before said, Mr Cavendish broke a flirtation clean off at its most interesting moment."
"Broke a flirtation clean off" — that verb choice is extraordinary.
It's not interrupted, not suspended — it's broken, like a branch or a bone.
Oliphant gives us the whole social ecology of the evening in one sentence — and then fractures it with music.
And that fracture is precisely where Cavendish's vulnerability becomes visible.
He is a man who depends on social fluency — on being able to work a room, to keep a flirtation running at exactly the right temperature.
A man going into Parliament cannot afford to be publicly stopped in his tracks by a pair of voices — however beautiful.
Mrs Woodburn's little observation later — "I shall be quite interested to watch you, Lucilla, when it comes to be your turn, and see how you manage" — that line has a needle in it.
She's watching Lucilla, yes — but the watching is also a warning.
Everyone in this circle understands that Cavendish's social fate is now somehow entangled with how Lucilla chooses to proceed.
The comedy is real, but underneath it is a quite cold-blooded power calculation.
And what Oliphant is so good at is keeping both registers alive at once — we laugh, and then we feel slightly uncomfortable that we laughed.
Cavendish thinks he is directing the scene — the polished future M.P., orbiting Lucilla with practised grace.
But Lucilla is assessing him the way a chess player considers a piece — useful, possibly, depending on the position of everything else on the board.
He doesn't know he's the piece.
And that gap — between his self-image and her actual assessment — is where the whole comedy of his situation lives.
It's also where his masculine respectability becomes precarious in a very specific way.
Cavendish's authority — as a man of Parliament, a man of society — rests on being seen to choose, not to be chosen.
The moment Lucilla starts weighing him as a political asset, the direction of power quietly reverses — and Oliphant knows exactly what she's doing.
She's rewriting the grammar of courtship from the inside, without any of the characters quite noticing.

That rewriting of grammar — and the question of who holds the real authority in any given social exchange — takes on a new dimension when we consider who else is hovering at the edges of Lucilla's world.

In the next part of our conversation, we're turning to Tom Marjoribanks — the cousin Lucilla has already decided to crush in the bud — and what his homecoming reveals about the limits of even her considerable reach.

segments.title: Tom's Homecoming: Duty, Desire, and the Limits of Lucilla's World

utterances.text: We've been talking about how masculine respectability cracks under social pressure in Carlingford.
Now I want to turn to a figure who arrives into Lucilla's carefully constructed world and almost immediately destabilises it — her cousin Tom.
Tom Marjoribanks is one of those characters who is almost entirely defined by what he cannot do.
He cannot navigate Miss Bury's social interrogation.
He cannot protect Lucilla at the very moment she needs a cousin who knows how to behave.
And Mrs Oliphant captures his humiliation with such precise, almost clinical comedy.
She writes —
"The unfortunate Tom grew red and then he grew green under this question and that awful look."
Red and then green — the physical register of social catastrophe, rendered in two colours.
What I love about that sentence is the rhythm of it — the doubling.
"Grew red and then he grew green" — she doesn't collapse those two stages into one.
You watch the humiliation unfold in real time, beat by beat, through colour.
And then that extraordinary parenthetical — "the amusing man was so much less brotherly than Tom."
It's devastating social commentary wrapped inside what reads as a neutral observation.
The barrister's laughter is called "unsympathetic" — and that single word does the moral work of a paragraph.
The theological dimension here is worth pausing on.
Miss Bury is the vicar's relative, and her question about belief in Jove is not simply eccentric — it is a social screening device.
In mid-Victorian Carlingford, religious orthodoxy and social respectability are effectively the same currency.
Which is why the narrator's description of Lucilla's recovery is so perfectly chosen.
Listen to what saves the situation —
"her courage and coolness, not to say her orthodoxy, were equal to the occasion."
Not to say her orthodoxy — slipped in almost as an afterthought, yet it is precisely what matters in that room.
And you feel the narrator's relish in that phrase, don't you.
Mrs Oliphant is genuinely fond of Lucilla and yet she never flatters her — she shows us exactly what tools Lucilla is working with and exactly how cold-blooded she is in deploying them.
"She gave her cousin a look which was still more terrible than Miss Bury's, and then she took affairs into her own hands."
That sequence — the look, then the action — is pure Lucilla.
She disciplines Tom with a glance and then simply absorbs the crisis into her management of the room.
What's fascinating is that this social near-disaster follows Lucilla into sleep.
The dream sequence in chapter eight is remarkable — and quite unusual for Oliphant's mode of narration.
Lucilla's anxieties take a gothic, shape-shifting form.
The scene is set up as follows —
"She dreamed that she stood at the altar by the side of the member for Carlingford, and that Mr Bury, with inflexible cruelty, insisted upon marrying her to Tom Marjoribanks instead."
"Inflexible cruelty" — applied to a vicar performing a wedding ceremony.
The comedy is savage because the cruelty is real — to be married to Tom rather than to secure Mr Cavendish's political future is, for Lucilla, a genuine catastrophe.
That's precisely right, and the political dimension of the dream shouldn't be overlooked.
Lucilla's nightmare conflates marriage and electoral outcome — they are, in her imagination, equivalently high stakes.
She cannot vote, cannot stand for Parliament, cannot exercise institutional power — but she has made herself indispensable to those who can.
The dream reveals that she knows this dependency — and fears the mechanisms by which it might be undone.
And then there's the second half of that dream, which I find almost funnier than the first.
The scene shifts to the hustings, and it is the amusing man — the unsympathetic barrister — who grins at her from the defeated candidate's position.
And what does he threaten her with — not scandal, not social ruin in the abstract — but that he would never forget the luncheon.
Mrs Oliphant writes that he said he would never forget "the luncheon that had been his first introduction to Carlingford."
For Lucilla, that luncheon is the emblem of everything she failed to control — and it haunts her precisely because control is everything.
Which brings us to one of the most quietly audacious moments in the novel — much later, when Lucilla confronts her own reflection.
Oliphant gives her this extraordinary passage where Lucilla looks into the mirror with her aunt and delivers a verdict on herself with total candour.
The lines are —

"I don't think I am quite so much gone off as I expected to be — though of course he will think me stouter — but it does not make any difference about Mr Ashburton being the right man for Carlingford."
The self-assessment is utterly unsentimental — and then the pivot is instant and complete.
Her own appearance is simply a variable to be accounted for, and then set aside in favour of the political calculation that actually matters to her.
What strikes me about that passage is the word "solemnity."
The narrator tells us that Lucilla "said the words with a certain solemnity" — about Mr Ashburton being the right man for the borough.
That solemnity is not ironic — or not entirely ironic.
Lucilla has a genuine political vocation, constrained entirely by her sex and her era, and the novel takes that vocation seriously even as it smiles at it.
And Aunt Jemima's speechlessness at the end of that scene is the perfect punctuation mark.
She has been physically steered — turned to face the mirror, then turned back again, then led upstairs — entirely at Lucilla's direction.
She cannot find words because Lucilla's logic, once you enter it, is perfectly coherent — and perfectly implacable.
That combination — comic surface, serious underneath — is what makes Lucilla one of the great Victorian protagonists.
So we've seen Lucilla manage crises, absorb humiliations, and steer entire rooms — including rooms in her own unconscious.
In our next segment, we ask what all of that management ultimately adds up to — the legacy of a woman who ran Carlingford's social world for years, entirely without official sanction.

segments.title: The Price of Influence: Legacy, Authority, and the Woman Who Orchestrated Society

utterances.text: We've been talking about the limits that press in on Lucilla from outside — Tom's return, desire, the claims of the personal.
But Lucilla's real genius, the thing that defines her across the whole novel, is her extraordinary gift for orchestration — for making things happen while appearing merely to preside.
That's what I want us to finish with: the architecture of her influence, the price she pays for it, and what the novel finally makes of the life she's built.
There's a passage in Chapter Twenty-Three that I keep returning to, because it captures Lucilla's mind at full stretch — and Oliphant's prose at full stretch to match it.

Lucilla has just grasped a new opportunity — a tangle involving the Archdeacon, a mysterious young man, and the prospect of engineering a marriage — and the narrator lays out her programme in one extraordinary sentence.

"To vanquish the Archdeacon, to pluck out from the darkness, and rehabilitate and set at his ease the mysterious adventurer... and to finish off by a glorious and triumphant marriage — not her own, it is true, but of her making, which was more to the purpose."
"Not her own, but of her making, which was more to the purpose."
That parenthesis is devastating — and the narrator delivers it with absolute deadpan precision.
Lucilla's own marriage is almost an afterthought beside the glory of authorship — of being the one who arranged it all.
And then that final phrase: "with the speed of lightning" — she makes out the whole programme in an instant, the moment she has the clue.
Oliphant is genuinely in awe of that cognitive speed, even as she's laughing at it.
What strikes me is that phrase "guided or seemed to guide" — that tiny qualification buried in the sentence.
The labyrinth may be real, or it may be a construction Lucilla has imposed on a perfectly ordinary situation.
Oliphant is never quite willing to tell us whether Lucilla's genius is genuine perception or magnificent self-delusion.
And that ambiguity is exactly what keeps the novel alive over a hundred and fifty years.
I want to bring in a passage from much later in the novel that I think shows how Lucilla's concept of power matures — becomes, if anything, more sophisticated.
By Chapter Thirty-Three, she has reached a kind of meta-level of control — the recognition that the highest exercise of management is knowing when not to manage.
The narrator puts it with characteristic compactness:
"she felt by instinct that now was the moment to make a high effort and leave things alone."
"A high effort" — to do nothing.
That is a very precise account of how institutional power actually operates at its most refined — not through visible exertion, but through the deliberate withholding of intervention.
Oliphant understood, I think, that the most durable authority is the kind that doesn't need to be seen to be acting.
James's point connects directly to something that happens structurally much later — Chapter Forty-Nine — that I find almost unbearably well judged.
Lucilla's father has been dead for years, his room closed, his bell long silent.
And then, at a pivotal moment, that bell rings again.
Listen to how Oliphant describes it:

"The old disused bell that had so often called Dr Marjoribanks up at night... began to peal through the silence, as if rung by a hand too impatient to notice what it was with which it made its summons."
"Too impatient to notice" — that bell doesn't know it's a ghost object.
The whole history of the father — his night calls, his authority, the household organised around his needs — returns in a single peal of sound.
It's Gothic, but it's also absolutely domestic — and that combination is very specifically Oliphant's register.
That moment stopped me cold on every re-reading.
Because the bell isn't just a Gothic flourish — it's a question about whose house this actually is.
Lucilla has spent the entire novel making Carlingford hers — managing it, shaping it, giving it a tone.
And the bell reminds her — and us — that she has been doing it in her father's house, under her father's name.
The novel is tender about this — not brutal — but it doesn't flinch from it either.
Which brings us, I think, to the comic masterpiece of the election chapters — because Oliphant doesn't let Lucilla be only poignant.

There is a scene in Chapter Thirty-Seven where Mr Ashburton has been talking earnestly about Reform — the burning political question of the day — and Lucilla has been listening with that particular brand of patient tolerance she reserves for men who have missed the point.
And then she redirects entirely:
"I was not thinking of Reform," she said, with that meekness which people assume when it is of no use being impatient.
"I was thinking what your colours were to be. I would not have anything to do with the old colours, for my part — they would be as bad as opinions, you know."
"As bad as opinions" — the ribbons matter more than the politics, and she is entirely right about this.
In a world where women could not vote, could not stand, could barely speak in a public room — controlling the visual grammar of a campaign was real power.
Lucilla is not trivialising the election.
She is operating in the one domain that was actually available to her.
And Oliphant shows the joke and the pathos in the same breath — which is technically very hard to do.
Lucilla's insistence that the colours must be new — "not the old colours" — is funny and principled and quietly desperate all at once.
She will not be given the old structures, so she will make her authority felt in the interstices — in colour, in tone, in the arrangement of a room.
That is the Lucilla the novel gives us from first page to last.
I think what I love most, coming to the end of the novel, is that Oliphant doesn't punish her.
So many novels of the period — and so many critics since — feel that an ambitious woman must be humbled or broken or shown her error.
Lucilla makes mistakes, yes — but the novel treats her intelligence as genuinely formidable, right to the last chapter.
She deserves better than Carlingford gave her, and I think Oliphant knew it.
That feels like the right note to end on — Oliphant knowing it, and trusting her readers to know it too.
This has been a genuinely rich conversation, and I'm deeply grateful to all three of you.
Eleanor, your attention to the architecture of Oliphant's sentences — the way a single parenthesis can carry a whole argument about female ambition — has been wonderful throughout.
James, you've kept us honest about the real world pressing in on the novel — the law, the politics, the specific constraints that shaped what Lucilla's intelligence could and couldn't do.
And Caroline, your reader's instinct — for what stops you cold, what makes you re-read a sentence — has been the beating heart of the discussion.
We've moved from the Thursday Evenings to the election, from a young woman's first great scheme to the peal of a ghost bell in an empty house.
Miss Marjoribanks is a novel that repays every re-reading — and if today has sent any of you back to it, we've done our work.
Thank you for listening.

c32:p41.text:
"The Archdeacon wants to make your acquaintance," said Miss
Marjoribanks. "Mr Cavendish—Mr Beverley. There, you know each other;
and when we are gone you can talk to each other if you like," Lucilla
added; "but in the meantime  you  are too far off, and  I  want the
Archdeacon. He is  so  much liked in Carlingford," she continued,
lowering her voice. "You can't think how glad we are to have him back
again.
c32:p41.summary: Lucilla briskly introduces the two men, directs Cavendish to remain silent, and publicly celebrates the Archdeacon's status in Carlingford.
c32:p41.best_quote: The Archdeacon wants to make your acquaintance. Mr Cavendish—Mr Beverley. There, you know each other

c38:p62.text:
But this news was naturally much more serious to Miss Marjoribanks when
she got upstairs, and had time to think of it. She would not have been
human if she had heard without emotion of the return of the man whom she
had once dreamed of as member for Carlingford, with the addition of
other dreams which had not been altogether without their sweetness.
c38:p62.summary: Lucilla recognizes that Mr Cavendish's return stirs emotions she thought past—he had been her dream candidate and romantic interest.
c38:p62.best_quote: She would not have been human if she had heard without emotion of the return of the man whom she had once dreamed of as member for Carlingford, with the addition of other dreams which had not been altogether without their sweetness.

c38:p50.text:
"Thank you all the same, papa, for bringing me the paper," said Lucilla. "It would have been a great deal worse if I had not known of it before I
saw him. I am sure I am very glad for one thing. He can't be married or
dead, as people used to say.
c38:p50.summary: Lucilla graciously thanks her father and notes that foreknowledge of the return is preferable to a surprise encounter.
c38:p50.best_quote: It would have been a great deal worse if I had not known of it before I saw him.

c50:p48.text:
It was to be Tom after all—after all the
archdeacons, doctors, generals, members of Parliament—after the ten
years and more in which she had not gone off—after the poor old
Doctor's grudge against the nephew whom he did not wish to inherit his
wealth, and Aunt Jemima's quiet wiles, and attempt to disappoint her
boy.
c50:p48.summary: The narrator catalogues the many suitors and obstacles Tom has overcome to finally win Lucilla.
c50:p48.best_quote: after all the archdeacons, doctors, generals, members of Parliament—after the ten years and more in which she had not gone off

c8:p44.text:
Lucilla uttered a scream of genuine alarm and dismay; and then she came
to herself, and saw the force of her position. She had it in her power
to turn the tables on the Rector, and she did not hesitate, as a weaker
woman might have done, out of consideration for anybody's feelings.
c8:p44.summary: Lucilla gasps in alarm at Mr Bury's suggestion, then quickly recognizes the opportunity to turn the tables on him.

c8:p56.text:
You may think the liberty is pleasant at first, but if you
had a Christian friend to watch over and take care of you——What is the
matter?" said the Rector, in great alarm. It was only that the poor
widow who was to have charge of Lucilla, according to his benevolent
intention, looked so like fainting, that Miss Marjoribanks jumped up
from her chair and rang the bell hastily.
c8:p56.summary: As Mr Bury outlines his plan, Mrs Mortimer looks ready to faint, forcing Lucilla to ring the bell and intervene with practical concern.

c8:p57.text:
It was not Lucilla's way to
lose time about anything; she took the poor woman by the shoulders and
all but lifted her to the sofa, where she was lying down with her bonnet
off when the Rector came to his senses. To describe the feelings with
which Mr Bury contemplated this little  entr'acte , which was not in his
programme, would be beyond our powers.
c8:p57.summary: Lucilla efficiently takes charge, helping the fainting Mrs Mortimer to the sofa while the Rector watches helplessly, unable to proceed with his address.

c8:p45.text:
"Do
you mean you have found some one for him to marry?" she asked, with a
look of artless surprise, bending her earnest gaze on Mr Bury's face.
c8:p45.summary: Lucilla feigns artless misunderstanding, asking if Mr Bury has found a remarriage prospect for her father.
c8:p45.best_quote: Do you mean you have found some one for him to marry?

c8:p69.text:
When he was gone Miss Marjoribanks felt the full importance of
her victory; and then, though she had not hesitated to sacrifice this
poor woman when it was necessary to have a victim, that moment was over,
and she had no pleasure in being cruel; on the contrary, she went and
sat by her patient, and talked, and was very kind to her; and after a
while heard all her story, and was more comforting than the Rector could
have been for his life.
c8:p69.summary: Once her victory is assured, Lucilla abandons her calculated coldness and becomes genuinely kind to the suffering Mrs Mortimer, sitting with her and offering comfort.

c9:p41.text:
"Lucilla," cried the unlucky fellow, "is it possible that you really
have misunderstood me all this time? Do you mean to say that you don't
know? Oh, Lucilla, listen just five minutes. It isn't because I am your
cousin. I wish to Heaven I was not your cousin, but some one you had
never seen before. I mean I want you to consent to—to—to—marry me,
Lucilla. That is what I mean.
c9:p41.summary: Tom finally explicitly proposes marriage, admitting his long-held love and his wish that he were not her cousin, begging Lucilla to listen to him.
c9:p41.best_quote: I mean I want you to consent to—to—to—marry me, Lucilla.

c2:p14.text:
Perhaps her course might be a little deficient in grace,
but grace, after all, is but a secondary quality; and, at all events,
Miss Marjoribanks went straight forward, leaving an unquestionable wake
behind her, and running down with indifference the little skiffs in her
way. She was possessed by nature of that kind of egotism, or rather
egoism, which is predestined to impress itself, by its perfect reality
and good faith, upon the surrounding world.
c2:p14.summary: Lucilla possesses a profound, unself-conscious egoism that impresses itself on others through its complete sincerity and lack of self-doubt.
c2:p14.best_quote: Miss Marjoribanks went straight forward, leaving an unquestionable wake behind her, and running down with indifference the little skiffs in her way

c28:p70.text:
"Hush," said Lucilla, "don't laugh, please; for I want to have a very
serious talk. I have been hearing about you from some very, very old
friends, Mr Cavendish—not anything about  this , you know," Miss
Marjoribanks added, waving her hand in the direction of Grove Street. And then Barbara Lake and everything connected with her vanished like a
shadow from the unfortunate man's mind.
c28:p70.summary: Lucilla indicates her knowledge concerns not Barbara but very old friends and past matters, causing Barbara to fade from Cavendish's mind entirely.
c28:p70.best_quote: "Hush," said Lucilla, "don't laugh, please; for I want to have a very serious talk. I have been hearing about you from some very, very old friends, Mr Cavendish—not anything about this, you know," Miss Marjoribanks added, waving her hand in the direction of Grove Street. And then Barbara Lake and everything connected with her vanished like a shadow from the unfortunate man's mind.

c38:p55.text:
It was actually Mr Cavendish who had come
home, and whose address to the electors of Carlingford, dated from Dover
on his return to England, the Doctor had just put into his daughter's
hand. But wonderful and unlooked-for as was the event, Lucilla, though
taken unawares, had not given in, nor shown any signs of weakness.
c38:p55.summary: The mysterious returned candidate is revealed to be Mr Cavendish, who has issued his political address to the Carlingford electors.
c38:p55.best_quote: It was actually Mr Cavendish who had come home, and whose address to the electors of Carlingford, dated from Dover on his return to England, the Doctor had just put into his daughter's hand.

c49:p43.text:
She was frightened at it herself before the words were out of her mouth,
and the effect it had upon Miss Marjoribanks was wonderful. She threw
her embroidery away, and looked Tom's mother keenly in the face. "I
don't think you know anybody who is fond of me, Aunt Jemima," she said;
"I don't suppose anybody is fond of me. Do you?" said Lucilla.
c49:p43.summary: Lucilla turns the tables on Aunt Jemima with a sharp question, suggesting she doesn't believe anyone is fond of her.
c49:p43.best_quote: "I don't think you know anybody who is fond of me, Aunt Jemima," she said; "I don't suppose anybody is fond of me. Do you?"

c1:p24.text:
On the contrary, a painful heaviness possessed him when he
became aware how little real sorrow was in his mind, and how small an
actual loss was this loss of his wife, which bulked before the world as
an event of just as much magnitude as the loss, for example, which poor
Mr Lake, the drawing-master, was at the same moment suffering.
c1:p24.summary: Dr Marjoribanks feels a painful heaviness realizing that his wife's death is truly no real loss to him, though the world treats it as significant.
c1:p24.best_quote: a painful heaviness possessed him when he became aware how little real sorrow was in his mind, and how small an actual loss was this loss of his wife, which bulked before the world as an event of just as much magnitude as the loss, for example, which poor Mr Lake, the drawing-master, was at the same moment suffering.

c24:p61.text:
"Tell me, for Heaven's sake, what you mean!" cried the Archdeacon. "You
do not think, surely, that I for a moment meant to imply that Helen
would waste a thought upon such a miscreant. Good Heavens, marry him! You must be raving. She would as soon think of—going for a soldier,"
said Mr Beverley, with a hoarse and perfectly unmirthful laugh, "or
doing anything else that was mad and unnatural.
c24:p61.summary: The Archdeacon vehemently denies that Mrs Mortimer could ever consider marrying Kavan, responding with shocked laughter and hyperbolic comparisons.
c24:p61.best_quote: Good Heavens, marry him! You must be raving. She would as soon think of—going for a soldier, said Mr Beverley, with a hoarse and perfectly unmirthful laugh, or doing anything else that was mad and unnatural.

c43:p53.text:
He was dead, and he had made an elaborate will, which was all as just
and righteous as a will could be; but after the will was read, it was
found out that everything named in it had disappeared like a bubble. Instead of being the richest, Dr Marjoribanks was one of the poorest
men in Carlingford when he shut his door behind him on that snowy night.
c43:p53.summary: The Doctor's will is just, but upon reading it, everything named has vanished. The Doctor was actually one of the poorest men in Carlingford.
c43:p53.best_quote: after the will was read, it was found out that everything named in it had disappeared like a bubble. Instead of being the richest, Dr Marjoribanks was one of the poorest men in Carlingford when he shut his door behind him on that snowy night

c49:p23.text:
That was what he came to, poor
man! after all his experiences; a man who was capable of so much better
things—a man even who, if he had made a right use of his opportunities,
might once have had as good a chance as any other of marrying Lucilla
herself. If there ever was an instance of chances thrown away and lost
opportunities, surely here was that lamentable example.
c49:p23.summary: The narrator laments that Mr Cavendish might have won Lucilla had he used his opportunities wisely; he exemplifies thrown-away chances.
c49:p23.best_quote: a man who was capable of so much better things—a man even who, if he had made a right use of his opportunities, might once have had as good a chance as any other of marrying Lucilla herself

c49:p26.text:
For the first time in her life she not
only did not know what she would do, but she did not know what she
wanted to do. There could now be no mistaking what Mr Ashburton's
intentions were. Up to a very recent time Lucilla had been able to take
refuge in her mourning, and conclude that she had no present occasion to
disturb herself. But now that calm was over.
c49:p26.summary: Lucilla recognises that Mr Ashburton intends a proposal and faces an unprecedented crisis of indecision about her true desires.
c49:p26.best_quote: For the first time in her life she not only did not know what she would do, but she did not know what she wanted to do

c10:p62.text:
It was when she was in this unhappy humour
that her eye fell upon Mr Cavendish, who was in the act of making the
appeal to Lucilla which we have already recorded. Barbara had never as
yet had a lover, but she had read an unlimited number of novels, which
came to nearly the same thing, and she saw at a glance that this was
somebody who resembled the indispensable hero.
c10:p62.summary: Barbara spots Mr Cavendish and, inspired by novel heroines, recognises him as the archetypal hero; she imagines how the humble heroine often wins him over rivals.
c10:p62.best_quote: Barbara had never as yet had a lover, but she had read an unlimited number of novels, which came to nearly the same thing

c11:p21.text:
"I shall be quite interested to watch  you , Lucilla, when it
comes to be your turn, and see how you manage," she went on, with a keen
look at Miss Marjoribanks; and Mr Cavendish laughed. He too looked at
her, and Lucilla felt herself in rather a delicate position: not that
she was agitated, as might have been the case had the future M.P. for
Carlingford "engaged her affections," as she herself would have said.
c11:p21.summary: Mrs Woodburn makes a pointed observation about how Lucilla will handle her own marriage, implying awareness of Mr Cavendish's interest and placing Lucilla in a delicate position.
c11:p21.best_quote: I shall be quite interested to watch you, Lucilla, when it comes to be your turn, and see how you manage

c11:p11.text:
"It was a great deal more than pleasant," said Mr Cavendish; "and as for
your conception of social politics, it is masterly," the future M.P.
added, in a tone which struck Lucilla as very significant; not that she
cared particularly about Mr Cavendish's meaning, but still, when a young
man who intends to go into Parliament congratulates a young lady upon
her statesmanlike views, and her conception of politics, it must be
confessed that it looks a little particular; and then, if that was what
he meant, it was no doubt Lucilla's duty to make up her mind.
c11:p11.summary: Mr Cavendish congratulates Lucilla on her statesmanlike views with a tone that suggests romantic interest, prompting Lucilla to recognize this may require her decision.
c11:p11.best_quote: your conception of social politics, it is masterly

c11:p30.text:
It was not that she was unduly flattered by Mr
Cavendish's attentions, as might have happened to an inexperienced young
woman; for Lucilla, with her attractions and genius, had not reached the
mature age of nineteen without receiving the natural homage of mankind
on several clearly-defined occasions. But then the present case had
various features peculiar to itself, which prevented Lucilla from
crushing it in the bud, as she had meant to do with her cousin's
ill-fated passion.
c11:p30.summary: The narrator reveals that Lucilla, experienced in receiving male attention, recognizes Mr Cavendish's case as different because of political considerations distinct from her cousin Tom's situation.

c10:p74.text:
But this
evening there could be no mistake about it. The words were arrested on
the very lips of the talkers; Mrs Woodburn paused in the midst of doing
Lucilla, and, as we have before said, Mr Cavendish broke a flirtation
clean off at its most interesting moment.
c10:p74.summary: The duet shocks the assembly into complete silence: conversations freeze, Mrs Woodburn ceases her mimicry, Cavendish abandons his flirtation—an unmissable moment.
c10:p74.best_quote: The words were arrested on the very lips of the talkers; Mrs Woodburn paused in the midst of doing Lucilla, and, as we have before said, Mr Cavendish broke a flirtation clean off at its most interesting moment.

c7:p48.text:
The unfortunate Tom grew red and then he grew green under this question
and that awful look. "No, Miss Bury, I can't say I do," he answered
humbly; and the amusing man was so much less brotherly than Tom that he
burst into unsympathetic laughter. As for Lucilla, it was the first real
check she had sustained in the beginning of her career.
c7:p48.summary: Tom is mortified by Miss Bury's question and admits he does not believe in Jove; the barrister laughs unkindly, and Lucilla faces her first real check.
c7:p48.best_quote: The unfortunate Tom grew red and then he grew green under this question and that awful look.

c7:p49.text:
There could not
have been a more unfortunate  contretemps , and there is no telling how
disastrous the effect might have been, had not her courage and
coolness, not to say her orthodoxy, been equal to the occasion. She gave
her cousin a look which was still more terrible than Miss Bury's, and
then she took affairs into her own hands.
c7:p49.summary: The narrator emphasizes that a damaging social disaster has occurred, but Lucilla's courage, coolness, and orthodoxy allow her to take control and repair the situation.
c7:p49.best_quote: There could not have been a more unfortunate contretemps, and there is no telling how disastrous the effect might have been, had not her courage and coolness, not to say her orthodoxy, been equal to the occasion.

c8:p27.text:
She dreamed that she stood at the altar by the side
of the member for Carlingford, and that Mr Bury, with inflexible
cruelty, insisted upon marrying her to Tom Marjoribanks instead; and
then the scene changed, and instead of receiving the salutations of Mr
Cavendish as M.P. for the borough, it was the amusing man, in the
character of the defeated candidate, who grinned and nodded at her, and
said from the hustings that he would never forget the luncheon that had
been his first introduction to Carlingford.
c8:p27.summary: Lucilla dreams of being forced to marry Tom instead of securing Mr Cavendish as M.P., and of public mockery about the luncheon incident.

c38:p52.text:
Tell him I shall
be  so  glad to see him, papa; though I have no reason to be glad, for
he was one of my  young  friends, you know, and he is sure to think I
have gone off." As she spoke, Lucilla turned Aunt Jemima, to whom she
had given her arm, quite round, that she might look into the great glass
over the mantelpiece: "I don't think I  am  quite so much gone off as I
expected to be," said Miss Marjoribanks, with candid impartiality;
"though of course he will think me stouter—but it does not make any
difference about Mr Ashburton being the right man for Carlingford." She
said the words with a certain solemnity, and turned Mrs John, who was so
much surprised as to be speechless, round again, and led her upstairs.
c38:p52.summary: Lucilla examines her appearance in the mirror with her aunt, admits to some aging but maintains that Mr Ashburton remains the right candidate regardless.
c38:p52.best_quote: I don't think I am quite so much gone off as I expected to be. Though of course he will think me stouter—but it does not make any difference about Mr Ashburton being the right man for Carlingford.

c23:p118.text:
To vanquish the Archdeacon, to pluck out from the darkness,
and rehabilitate and set at his ease the mysterious adventurer, whom, to
be sure,  she could not say she knew —for Lucilla was very careful,
even in her own thoughts, not to commit herself on this subject—and to
finish off by a glorious and triumphant marriage—not her own, it is
true, but of her making, which was more to the purpose—such was the
programme she made out for herself with the speed of lightning, the
moment she had laid hold of the clue which guided or seemed to guide her
through the labyrinth.
c23:p118.summary: Lucilla immediately conceives an ambitious three-fold plan: overcoming the Archdeacon's influence, redeeming Kavan, and orchestrating a triumphant reconciliation.
c23:p118.best_quote: To vanquish the Archdeacon, to pluck out from the darkness, and rehabilitate and set at his ease the mysterious adventurer, whom, to be sure, she could not say she knew—for Lucilla was very careful, even in her own thoughts, not to commit herself on this subject—and to finish off by a glorious and triumphant marriage—not her own, it is true, but of her making, which was more to the purpose—such was the programme she made out for herself with the speed of lightning, the moment she had laid hold of the clue which guided or seemed to guide her through the labyrinth.

c33:p16.text:
Up to this
time she had managed everything herself, which was comparatively easy;
but she felt by instinct that now was the moment to make a high effort
and leave things alone. And it may be added that nothing but an inherent
sense of doing the right thing under the circumstances could have
inspired Miss Marjoribanks to the crowning achievement of keeping out of
the way.
c33:p16.summary: Lucilla recognizes that her usual direct management would be wrong; instead, she must deliberately refrain from intervening—a higher achievement of control through non-action.
c33:p16.best_quote: she felt by instinct that now was the moment to make a high effort and leave things alone

c49:p71.text:
The old disused bell that had so often called Dr
Marjoribanks up at night, and which hung near the door of the old
Doctor's room, just over the drawing-room, began to peal through the
silence, as if rung by a hand too impatient to notice what it was with
which it made its summons.
c49:p71.summary: The long-disused bell of Lucilla's late father summons from above, pealing urgently as if rung by an impatient hand.
c49:p71.best_quote: The old disused bell that had so often called Dr Marjoribanks up at night, and which hung near the door of the old Doctor's room, just over the drawing-room, began to peal through the silence, as if rung by a hand too impatient to notice what it was with which it made its summons

c37:p58.text:
Lucilla smiled compassionately, and with the gentlest tolerance, at this
wild suggestion. "I was not thinking of Reform," she said, with that
meekness which people assume when it is of no use being impatient. "I
was thinking what your colours were to be. I would not have anything to
do with the old colours, for my part—they would be as bad as opinions,
you know. You may laugh, but I am quite in earnest," said Miss
Marjoribanks.
c37:p58.summary: Lucilla reveals that the important matter is not Reform but choosing campaign colors (ribbons), which she insists must be new, not the tired old blue and yellow.
